title: dBi, dBd, dBm: RF Gain and Power Units
h1: Antenna gain and RF power — dBi, dBd, dBm
description: 0 dBd = 2.15 dBi. 0 dBm = 1 mW = −30 dBW. Link budgets live on these dB conversions — miss one, misplace an antenna.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: dB is a ratio. Reference matters. dBi vs dBd differs by 2.15 dB forever.
body: Antenna gain and RF power sit on decibel scales that reference different quantities. Getting the reference right is what separates a working link from a dead one.

> dB = 10 log₁₀(P₂/P₁)
> dBi = gain over isotropic radiator
> dBd = gain over half-wave dipole
> dBi − dBd = 2.15 dB (a dipole's own gain over isotropic)
> dBm = 10 log₁₀(P / 1 mW); dBW = 10 log₁₀(P / 1 W); dBm = dBW + 30
1 W = 30 dBm = 0 dBW. 100 mW = 20 dBm. 1 µW = −30 dBm. Home Wi-Fi router transmit: 15–20 dBm. 5 dBi antenna = 2.85 dBd. 24 dBi parabolic dish ≈ 22 dBd.

TX 20 dBm, antenna 5 dBi, cable −2 dB, path loss −90 dB, RX antenna 5 dBi, RX sensitivity −80 dBm. Received power = 20 + 5 − 2 − 90 + 5 = −62 dBm. Margin = −62 − (−80) = 18 dB. Read the TX antenna spec as 5 dBd instead: add 2.15 dB, redo — 20 dB margin.
Reference matters. dBi > dBd by 2.15. dBm = dBW + 30.

faqs.q: Is dB the same as dBA?
faqs.a: No — dBA is A-weighted sound pressure, unrelated to RF.
